title: Job 37:14–24
context: Elihu speaks directly to Job, urging him to stop and consider God's wondrous works. He asks a series of questions about the clouds, lightning, wind, and sky that Job cannot answer, and says no one can make a case before God because of darkness. He ends by saying that people cannot reach the Almighty, who is great in power and justice, and that people should revere him. Elihu's questions anticipate the LORD's questions in chapters 38–41. His closing words are his own, not the book's last word, since the LORD himself speaks next (38:1).

verses.text: “Listen to this, Job. Stand still, and consider the wondrous works of God.
verses.arminianNotes: "Listen to this, Job." Arminian readers see Elihu calling Job to "Stand still, and consider the wondrous works of God," urging reflection rather than complaint.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the call to stillness before God's works prepares the reader for the LORD's speeches. Elihu's appeal is fitting, though the LORD will speak with far greater authority.

verses.text: Do you know how God controls them, and causes the lightning of his cloud to shine?
verses.arminianNotes: "Do you know how God controls them." Arminian readers see Elihu beginning a string of questions meant to humble Job by showing how little he knows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu's questions resemble the LORD's in chapter 38. The similarity raises the question of how the two relate, which interpreters answer differently.

verses.text: Do you know the workings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him who is perfect in knowledge?
verses.arminianNotes: "Do you know the workings of the clouds." Arminian readers note that Elihu calls God "him who is perfect in knowledge," the same phrase he seemed to use of himself in 36:4.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that whatever Elihu meant in 36:4, here the phrase rightly belongs to God. Only God's knowledge is complete. Both traditions treat that as shared ground.

verses.text: You whose clothing is warm when the earth is still by reason of the south wind?
verses.arminianNotes: "You whose clothing is warm when the earth is still by reason of the south wind?" Arminian readers see Elihu pointing to Job's experience of heat to show that he only feels the weather without controlling it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the contrast between Job's limited experience and God's control. Job knows his clothes are warm, but not how the winds are governed.

verses.text: Can you, with him, spread out the sky, which is strong as a cast metal mirror?
verses.arminianNotes: "Can you, with him, spread out the sky." Arminian readers see Elihu asking whether Job could help God make the sky, which is "strong as a cast metal mirror."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the image describes the sky as it appeared to ancient observers. The point is God's creative power, which Job cannot share.

verses.text: Teach us what we will tell him, for we can’t make our case by reason of darkness.
verses.arminianNotes: "Teach us what we will tell him." Arminian readers hear irony: Elihu challenges Job to teach them what to say to God, since "we can’t make our case by reason of darkness."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job had longed to argue his case before God (13:3). Elihu replies that human darkness makes such a case impossible. The LORD will later invite Job to answer him (40:2).

verses.text: Will it be told him that I would speak? Or should a man wish that he were swallowed up?
verses.arminianNotes: "Will it be told him that I would speak?" Arminian readers see Elihu suggesting that demanding a hearing with God is dangerous, like wishing to be "swallowed up."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu warns against presuming to speak to God on one's own terms. Yet the LORD will in fact answer Job, which the book presents as a gracious turn.

verses.text: Now men don’t see the light which is bright in the skies, but the wind passes, and clears them.
verses.arminianNotes: "Now men don’t see the light which is bright in the skies." Arminian readers see an image of light hidden by clouds until the wind clears them, perhaps hinting that God's glory will soon be revealed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the image can be read as pointing toward a coming revelation. They hold that reading loosely, since Elihu does not explain it, but the next chapter brings the LORD's appearing.

verses.text: Out of the north comes golden splendor. With God is awesome majesty.
verses.arminianNotes: "Out of the north comes golden splendor." Arminian readers see Elihu describing a radiant brightness and confessing, "With God is awesome majesty."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the speech rises to its climax in God's majesty. Both traditions treat this confession of God's glory as shared ground.

verses.text: We can’t reach the Almighty. He is exalted in power. In justice and great righteousness, he will not oppress.
verses.arminianNotes: "We can’t reach the Almighty." Arminian readers see Elihu affirming both God's greatness and his justice: "In justice and great righteousness, he will not oppress."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this is Elihu's close, not the book's last word. The LORD, whom Elihu says cannot be reached, will speak directly to Job in the next chapter (38:1).

verses.text: Therefore men revere him. He doesn’t regard any who are wise of heart.”
verses.arminianNotes: "Therefore men revere him." Arminian readers see Elihu's conclusion that the right response to God is reverence, not proud claims to wisdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God "doesn’t regard any who are wise of heart," meaning those wise in their own eyes. Compare Job 28:28: "the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom."
